contentHtml:
ETHIOPIA—The Ethiopian government, in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, and Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) partners, has launched a polio vaccination campaign targeting more than 11.3 million children across five regions to prevent the spread of poliovirus.

The campaign covers Addis Ababa, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, South Ethiopia, and Southwest Ethiopia.

It will run in two rounds, with the first taking place from November 21 to 24, followed by a second round from December 18 to 21.

Speaking at the launch in Arba Minch, South Ethiopia Region, Dr Loveday Nkwogu delivered a joint statement on behalf of Professor Francis Kasolo, WHO Representative to Ethiopia.

He called for coordinated efforts among government authorities, healthcare workers, community leaders and parents to ensure that every eligible child receives the vaccine.

He warned that poliovirus continues to threaten children in communities where vaccination coverage remains low, despite progress in controlling the disease.

House-to-house vaccination and surveillance

Health workers and community volunteers will conduct house-to-house visits to administer polio vaccines to eligible children.

During these visits, teams will also identify children who have never received routine vaccines or have missed scheduled doses and refer them to nearby immunisation services.

WHO has deployed 28 central and field staff to support implementation.

Its technical teams have assisted with campaign coordination, advocacy, operational planning and training of health workers and supervisors at national and regional levels.

The organisation has also trained supervisors and independent monitors to use Open Data Kit (ODK) for digital data collection and monitoring.

In addition, it has supported lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) training, campaign supervision, data management and community engagement to assess vaccination coverage and service quality.

Variant poliovirus outbreaks prompt response

Although Ethiopia remains free of wild poliovirus, circulating variant poliovirus continues to pose a public health threat, particularly in communities with low immunisation coverage and high population movement.

During 2026, cases of circulating variant poliovirus type 1 were reported in Gambella, Oromia and South Ethiopia.

The outbreaks have prompted vaccination campaigns in affected areas, including Gambella, Benishangul-Gumuz and parts of Oromia, where previous interventions reached more than one million children.

Alongside vaccination, WHO and its partners are calling for stronger surveillance to detect poliovirus transmission early.

High-quality acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance and environmental monitoring remain important for identifying infections and guiding rapid outbreak responses.

WHO continues to support the Ethiopian government with technical and operational assistance in campaign planning, coordination, monitoring, supervision, and disease surveillance.

The partnership forms part of ongoing global efforts to interrupt poliovirus transmission and strengthen routine immunisation systems.
